approachQuestion.prompt:
Rain Gauge Profile

An array height gives the nonnegative integer heights of n adjacent solid columns, each one unit wide. Rain falls over the profile, and water runs off beyond either outer end. Return the total number of unit squares of water retained above the columns after settling. Equivalently, column i retains max(0,min(max(height[0:i+1]),max(height[i:n]))-height[i]). Do not change height.

Constraints: 0 <= n=height.length <= 200000; 0 <= height[i] <= 1000000000. Use signed 64-bit accumulated volume.

Example 1: height=[3,0,1,0,2] -> 5 (depths 0,2,1,2,0).
Example 2: height=[2,0,2] -> 2.
Example 3: height=[1,2,3] -> 0.
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Keep inward indices l,r, maxima leftMax,rightMax initially zero, and volume zero. While l<=r, update both maxima with height[l] and height[r]. If leftMax<=rightMax, add leftMax-height[l] and increment l; otherwise add rightMax-height[r] and decrement r.
options.feedback: The smaller established maximum has a guaranteed boundary on the opposite side. Its current column depth is therefore final even if taller boundaries appear later.

options.text: Build arrays of prefix maxima and suffix maxima, then sum min(prefix[i],suffix[i])-height[i] over every column.
options.feedback: The formula is correct at every position, but the full maximum arrays can be replaced by two running boundary values.

options.text: For each interior column add max(0,min(height[i-1],height[i+1])-height[i]); sum those local depths.
options.feedback: For [3,0,0,3], the two zero columns each hold 3 units, but local neighbors make this rule return zero.

options.text: Use the same running-max algorithm, but finalize the left column when leftMax>=rightMax and the right column otherwise.
options.feedback: For [3,0,1], it processes the left side using boundary 3 and overcounts the middle depth as 3, even though the right boundary only supports depth 1.

feedback.reason: Finalize water depth from the side whose established maximum is lower, retaining boundary summaries instead of full prefix/suffix arrays.
details: Initialize left and right indices at the ends and both running maxima to zero. While the indices have not crossed, include each current endpoint height in its side's maximum. Finalize the column on the side with the smaller running maximum, add that maximum minus the column height, and move only that side inward; use the left side on ties.

The smaller running maximum has an already sufficient opposite boundary, so its column's water level is settled. Move only that side; finalizing from current heights alone would ignore taller boundaries already passed.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is column count. The method is iterative, creates no prefix/suffix arrays or input copies, and uses no recursion, hashing, or amortized container operations.
constraints: Analyze this fixed method regardless of your answer to question 1; choose the tightest pair.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Finalize one column per iteration using two running maxima.
details: Exactly one column is finalized per iteration and there are n columns, so the time is linear, including profiles with no retained water. Two indices, two maxima, and a 64-bit volume accumulator are fixed auxiliary storage.
